questions.prompt: An enzyme-controlled reaction is investigated at 30 °C. (a) Explain how enzyme structure determines specificity. (3) (b) Explain why increasing temperature initially increases rate. (2) (c) Explain why very high temperatures reduce the rate. (2)
hints: Link tertiary structure to the active site.
questions.solution: (a) The tertiary structure forms an active site with a specific shape/chemical environment complementary to the substrate. (b) Higher temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, increasing successful enzyme-substrate collisions. (c) Bonds maintaining tertiary structure are disrupted, changing the active site and causing denaturation. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: An enzyme-controlled reaction is investigated at 50 °C. (a) Explain how enzyme structure determines specificity. (3) (b) Explain why increasing temperature initially increases rate. (2) (c) Explain why very high temperatures reduce the rate. (2)
hints: Link tertiary structure to the active site.
questions.solution: (a) The tertiary structure forms an active site with a specific shape/chemical environment complementary to the substrate. (b) Higher temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, increasing successful enzyme-substrate collisions. (c) Bonds maintaining tertiary structure are disrupted, changing the active site and causing denaturation. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: An enzyme-controlled reaction is investigated at 30 °C. (a) Explain how enzyme structure determines specificity. (3) (b) Explain why increasing temperature initially increases rate. (2) (c) Explain why very high temperatures reduce the rate. (2)
hints: Link tertiary structure to the active site.
questions.solution: (a) The tertiary structure forms an active site with a specific shape/chemical environment complementary to the substrate. (b) Higher temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, increasing successful enzyme-substrate collisions. (c) Bonds maintaining tertiary structure are disrupted, changing the active site and causing denaturation. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: An enzyme-controlled reaction is investigated at 30 °C. (a) Explain how enzyme structure determines specificity. (3) (b) Explain why increasing temperature initially increases rate. (2) (c) Explain why very high temperatures reduce the rate. (2)
hints: Link tertiary structure to the active site.
questions.solution: (a) The tertiary structure forms an active site with a specific shape/chemical environment complementary to the substrate. (b) Higher temperature increases kinetic energy and collision frequency, increasing successful enzyme-substrate collisions. (c) Bonds maintaining tertiary structure are disrupted, changing the active site and causing denaturation. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: An electron micrograph shows a cell structure measuring 2.4 cm on the image at a magnification of $\times12000$. (a) Calculate the actual size in $\mu$m. (3) (b) State one advantage of electron microscopy over light microscopy. (2) (c) Explain one function of a membrane-bound organelle. (2)
hints: Use actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
questions.solution: (a) Actual size $=2.4/12000$ cm $=2.000\,\mu$m after unit conversion. (b) Electron microscopes have greater resolving power because electrons have a much shorter wavelength. (c) Credit a named organelle with a correct function. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: An electron micrograph shows a cell structure measuring 2.4 cm on the image at a magnification of $\times12000$. (a) Calculate the actual size in $\mu$m. (3) (b) State one advantage of electron microscopy over light microscopy. (2) (c) Explain one function of a membrane-bound organelle. (2)
hints: Use actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
questions.solution: (a) Actual size $=2.4/12000$ cm $=2.000\,\mu$m after unit conversion. (b) Electron microscopes have greater resolving power because electrons have a much shorter wavelength. (c) Credit a named organelle with a correct function. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: An electron micrograph shows a cell structure measuring 4.8 cm on the image at a magnification of $\times24000$. (a) Calculate the actual size in $\mu$m. (3) (b) State one advantage of electron microscopy over light microscopy. (2) (c) Explain one function of a membrane-bound organelle. (2)
hints: Use actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
questions.solution: (a) Actual size $=4.8/24000$ cm $=2.000\,\mu$m after unit conversion. (b) Electron microscopes have greater resolving power because electrons have a much shorter wavelength. (c) Credit a named organelle with a correct function. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A population becomes geographically isolated. (a) Explain how isolation can lead to speciation. (5) (b) Explain how natural selection changes allele frequencies. (3) (c) State one method used to estimate abundance of an immobile species. (1)
hints: No gene flow is the key consequence of isolation.
Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies.
questions.solution: (a) Isolation prevents gene flow; different mutations/selection pressures and genetic drift cause allele-frequency divergence; reproductive isolation eventually develops. (b) Individuals with advantageous heritable alleles have greater reproductive success, so those alleles increase in frequency. (c) Quadrat sampling. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

hints: No gene flow is the key consequence of isolation.
Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies.
questions.solution: (a) Isolation prevents gene flow; different mutations/selection pressures and genetic drift cause allele-frequency divergence; reproductive isolation eventually develops. (b) Individuals with advantageous heritable alleles have greater reproductive success, so those alleles increase in frequency. (c) Quadrat sampling. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: A population becomes geographically isolated. (a) Explain how isolation can lead to speciation. (5) (b) Explain how natural selection changes allele frequencies. (3) (c) State one method used to estimate abundance of an immobile species. (1)
hints: No gene flow is the key consequence of isolation.
Selection acts on phenotypes but changes allele frequencies.

questions.prompt: A mammal has a high metabolic rate. (a) Explain two adaptations of an efficient gas-exchange surface. (4) (b) Explain how haemoglobin helps transport oxygen. (3) (c) Explain why tissue fluid forms at the arterial end of a capillary. (3)
hints: Think about partial pressure and reversible binding.
questions.solution: (a) Large surface area and a short diffusion distance/steep concentration gradient increase diffusion. (b) Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly; cooperative binding and changes in partial pressure aid loading/unloading. (c) Hydrostatic pressure exceeds the opposing oncotic pressure, forcing water and small solutes out while cells/proteins remain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A mammal has a high metabolic rate. (a) Explain two adaptations of an efficient gas-exchange surface. (4) (b) Explain how haemoglobin helps transport oxygen. (3) (c) Explain why tissue fluid forms at the arterial end of a capillary. (3)
hints: Think about partial pressure and reversible binding.
questions.solution: (a) Large surface area and a short diffusion distance/steep concentration gradient increase diffusion. (b) Haemoglobin binds oxygen reversibly; cooperative binding and changes in partial pressure aid loading/unloading. (c) Hydrostatic pressure exceeds the opposing oncotic pressure, forcing water and small solutes out while cells/proteins remain. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1]

questions.prompt: A plant is transferred from low light intensity to high light intensity. (a) Explain how the light-dependent reaction produces ATP and reduced NADP. (4) (b) Explain how these products are used in the Calvin cycle. (3) (c) State one factor that could become limiting at high light intensity. (1)
hints: Link ATP/reduced NADP to the Calvin cycle.
questions.solution: (a) Light excites electrons; electron transfer releases energy used to pump protons; a proton gradient drives ATP synthase; electrons/protons reduce NADP. (b) ATP supplies energy and reduced NADP supplies hydrogen/electrons for reduction of GP to TP and regeneration processes. (c) e.g. carbon dioxide concentration or temperature. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1]

(4) (b) Explain how these products are used in the Calvin cycle. (3) (c) State one factor that could become limiting at high light intensity. (1)
hints: Link ATP/reduced NADP to the Calvin cycle.
questions.solution: (a) Light excites electrons; electron transfer releases energy used to pump protons; a proton gradient drives ATP synthase; electrons/protons reduce NADP. (b) ATP supplies energy and reduced NADP supplies hydrogen/electrons for reduction of GP to TP and regeneration processes. (c) e.g. carbon dioxide concentration or temperature. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1]

questions.prompt: A pathogen enters the body for the first time. (a) Describe the primary immune response involving B lymphocytes. (5) (b) Explain why a second exposure usually produces a faster response. (2) (c) Explain one way vaccination can reduce spread through a population. (2)

questions.solution: (a) A specific B cell is activated by antigen/helper T-cell signalling, undergoes clonal expansion, and differentiates into plasma cells producing specific antibody and memory cells. (b) Memory cells are already present and rapidly form plasma cells. (c) More immune individuals reduce transmission chains and the effective reproduction of the pathogen. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.solution: (a) A specific B cell is activated by antigen/helper T-cell signalling, undergoes clonal expansion, and differentiates into plasma cells producing specific antibody and memory cells. (b) Memory cells are already present and rapidly form plasma cells. (c) More immune individuals reduce transmission chains and the effective reproduction of the pathogen. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype is 0.36. (a) Calculate the recessive allele frequency $q$. (2) (b) Calculate the expected heterozygote frequency. (2) (c) State two assumptions of the Hardy–Weinberg model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) $q^2=0.36$, so $q=0.60$. (b) $p=1-q=0.40$ and $2pq=0.480$. (c) Any two: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.solution: (a) $q^2=0.49$, so $q=0.70$. (b) $p=1-q=0.30$ and $2pq=0.420$. (c) Any two: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of the homozygous recessive genotype is 0.64. (a) Calculate the recessive allele frequency $q$. (2) (b) Calculate the expected heterozygote frequency. (2) (c) State two assumptions of the Hardy–Weinberg model. (2)
questions.solution: (a) $q^2=0.64$, so $q=0.80$. (b) $p=1-q=0.20$ and $2pq=0.320$. (c) Any two: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.solution: (a) $q^2=0.36$, so $q=0.60$. (b) $p=1-q=0.40$ and $2pq=0.480$. (c) Any two: large population, random mating, no selection, no mutation, no migration. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1 B1]

questions.prompt: Two groups of organisms have sample sizes 12 and 12, with mean values 24.2 and 20.1. (a) State a suitable statistical test for comparing the means of two independent groups when the data are approximately normally distributed. (1) (b) Explain what a p-value below 0.05 means. (2) (c) Give two improvements to the experimental design. (2)
hints: Match the test to two independent means.
A p-value is conditional on the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: (a) Independent-samples t-test. (b) If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of obtaining a difference at least this extreme is below 5%; the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. (c) e.g. increase sample size, randomise allocation/sampling, control confounding variables, repeat measurements. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1]

questions.prompt: Two groups of organisms have sample sizes 15 and 15, with mean values 23.8 and 21.0. (a) State a suitable statistical test for comparing the means of two independent groups when the data are approximately normally distributed. (1) (b) Explain what a p-value below 0.05 means. (2) (c) Give two improvements to the experimental design. (2)
hints: Match the test to two independent means.
A p-value is conditional on the null hypothesis.
questions.solution: (a) Independent-samples t-test. (b) If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of obtaining a difference at least this extreme is below 5%; the result is statistically significant at the 5% level. (c) e.g. increase sample size, randomise allocation/sampling, control confounding variables, repeat measurements. [M1 A1 B1 M1 A1]
